Data Science, Machine Learning and AI sit on top of a software toolkit.

You do **not** need to become an expert software engineer in every tool. You do need enough fluency that the tools stop blocking your reasoning.

```text
                         DATA / AI WORK
                              │
        ┌──────────┬──────────┼──────────┬───────────┐
        ▼          ▼          ▼          ▼           ▼
     Python       SQL         R       Git/GitHub   Linux/CLI
        │          │          │          │           │
        └──────────┴──────────┴────┬─────┴───────────┘
                                   ▼
                           Spark / Big Data
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to use this section
Each article is intentionally short. Learn the **mental model and vocabulary here**, then follow the classified resources for deeper learning and practice.
:::

## Learning map

| Area | First objective | Then learn |
|---|---|---|
| Python | Write clear small programs | NumPy, pandas, algorithms |
| SQL | Query relational tables | windows, CTEs, analytical patterns |
| R | Think in vectors/data frames | tidyverse, modeling, Quarto |
| Git | Understand snapshots/branches | collaboration and recovery |
| GitHub | repositories and PRs | Actions, Pages, portfolio |
| Linux/CLI | navigate and compose commands | servers, processes, environments |
| Spark | think distributed | PySpark DataFrames and performance |

## Suggested order for a Data Scientist

```text
Python ★
SQL ★
Git/GitHub ★
Linux/CLI ★★
R ★★       ← especially statistics/research-heavy work
Spark ★★★  ← when data/compute becomes distributed
```

The stars indicate **learning order**, not importance or difficulty.

## One principle

> **Learn tools by building things with them.**

Reading gives vocabulary. Practice creates fluency. Projects reveal what you actually understand.
